# Interview questions at Dartmouth Health | aNewJob

Source: https://anewjob.com/interview-questions/at-dartmouth-health

Interview prep · Companies

# Interview questions at Dartmouth Health

Dartmouth Health says its purpose is to improve the health and well-being of patients, employees, and communities. Its careers site names founding values of partnership, kindness, community, and service, and it emphasizes teamwork, clinical excellence, access, and respect for the dignity, background and story of every patient. The hiring process varies by role and location, so check your posting and your recruiter's instructions, and note that the steps below are labeled by where they apply.

## How Dartmouth Health hires

- Apply online for an open position (DHMC and Clinics). You'll get an automatic confirmation email. Don't also email, fax, or mail a resume. You can apply to more than one position if you meet each one's minimum qualifications, which are listed on the posting. Applications can't be edited after submission, and temporaries/travelers apply as external applicants.

- Application review (DHMC and Clinics): the Recruitment team reviews applications daily and contacts only applicants whose skills best match current needs and the position's requirements. You can check your status anytime in your online application profile. Applications stay on file indefinitely, so you can reapply when another role fits.

- Recruiter phone screening (Cheshire Medical Center, a Dartmouth Health member): if you appear to be a potential fit, a recruiter calls you.

- Interviews (Cheshire Medical Center): after the screen, recruiters may schedule online or in-person interviews. Salary and the job description are typically discussed during the interview.

- Hiring decision and offer (DHMC and Clinics): time to hire varies. The hiring department makes the final decision and Recruitment extends the formal offer. For internal transfers, the hiring supervisor contacts your current supervisor once you pass the interview stage.

- Pre-placement drug and health screening (DHMC and Clinics, all new hires): every offer is contingent on passing a pre-placement drug screen. You schedule the health screening with Occupational Medicine as soon as you receive your offer letter. It includes a urine drug screen, a review of immunizations/titers, and TB testing if needed.

- Background check and health evaluation (Cheshire Medical Center): offers are contingent on both, and the New Hampshire background check can take up to 3 weeks.

- Orientation (Cheshire Medical Center): all new employees attend general and online orientation, and newly licensed nurses also complete a nursing residency program.

The process varies by role and location.

Question 1

## Why do you want to work in health care, and why this organization?

What they're asking: Tests whether your motivation fits the stated purpose of improving the health and well-being of patients, employees, and communities.

### Sample answer

Situation: When I was [your background, e.g., a caregiver for a family member / working in a previous role], I saw how much a coordinated, caring team changes someone's experience. Task: I wanted a career where my daily work directly supports people's well-being. Action: I took on [specific role, volunteer work, or training], where I [what you did], and I researched employers whose stated purpose matches that goal. Result: I learned that I do my best work when I'm helping patients and my colleagues at the same time. That's why this [role title] appeals to me. I want to bring my skills in [your strengths] to a team that cares about patients, employees, and the community, and keep growing in the process.

Question 2

## Tell me about a time you worked as part of a team to achieve a goal.

What they're asking: Assesses partnership and teamwork, which are among the values and principles Dartmouth Health emphasizes.

### Sample answer

Situation: At [previous workplace], our unit/team was short-staffed during [busy period] and a deadline for [goal] was at risk. Task: I needed to help the team deliver without sacrificing quality. Action: I met briefly with my colleagues, we mapped out who was strongest at which tasks, and I volunteered to take [specific tasks]. I also checked in with teammates midway to see who needed support and shifted my work accordingly. Result: We completed [outcome, e.g., all tasks on time] and [measurable result, e.g., no errors reported]. I learned that clear communication and sharing the load make a team stronger, and I carry that approach into every role I take.

Question 3

## Describe a time you showed kindness to someone who was frustrated or upset.

What they're asking: Probes the value of kindness and how you treat patients, visitors, and coworkers under stress.

### Sample answer

Situation: At [workplace], a [patient/customer/family member] became upset because of [a long wait / confusing information]. Task: I needed to help them feel heard while still doing my job accurately. Action: I stopped what I was doing, made eye contact, and let them explain without interrupting. I apologized for the frustration, explained what I could do, and gave them a clear next step. I also followed up with [colleague/department] so they wouldn't have to repeat their story. Result: They calmed down, thanked me, and [outcome, e.g., left with the answer they needed]. It reminded me that a few minutes of patience and empathy can change someone's whole experience.

Question 4

## Tell me about a time you contributed to your community, inside or outside of work.

What they're asking: Connects to the value of community and the goal of improving the well-being of the communities served.

### Sample answer

Situation: In [year], I noticed that [community need, e.g., local families struggled to access a resource]. Task: I wanted to help in a practical way alongside my regular responsibilities. Action: I joined [organization/event], recruited [number] others to help, and took responsibility for [specific tasks, e.g., scheduling volunteers, organizing supplies]. I made time each [week/month] and kept in touch with the people we served so we could adjust to their needs. Result: We [measurable outcome, e.g., supported 100 people / raised $X], and I built relationships that continue today. I learned that community impact comes from showing up consistently, and I'd like to keep serving in that spirit.

Question 5

## Give an example of when you went above and beyond to serve someone.

What they're asking: Evaluates the value of service and your willingness to put others' needs first.

### Sample answer

Situation: At [workplace], a [patient/client/coworker] needed [help with something outside my normal duties] right as my shift was ending. Task: I had to decide whether to hand it off or make sure it was resolved properly. Action: I stayed [short amount of time], found out exactly what they needed, and contacted [appropriate person/department] to arrange it. I wrote clear handoff notes so nothing was missed and checked back the next day. Result: The issue was resolved, the person told [supervisor/me] how much it meant to them, and my team adopted the same handoff approach afterward. For me, service means owning the problem until the person is truly helped, while still following proper procedures.

Question 6

## Tell me about a time you worked with someone whose background or experience was very different from yours. How did you show respect?

What they're asking: Tests respect for the dignity, background and story of every patient, a stated emphasis.

### Sample answer

Situation: At [workplace], I supported a [patient/client/coworker] whose [culture, language, age, or life circumstances] was very different from mine, and our first conversation felt awkward. Task: I wanted them to feel respected and understood, not judged or rushed. Action: I asked open questions about their preferences, listened without assuming, and used [interpreter/plain language/extra time] so they could share their story. I adjusted my approach based on what they told me and explained each step before I did it. Result: They became more comfortable, shared information that helped us [outcome], and gave positive feedback. I learned that curiosity and listening are the fastest ways to treat people with dignity.

Question 7

## Describe a time you caught a mistake or improved the quality of your work or your team's work.

What they're asking: Looks at commitment to clinical excellence and attention to quality and safety.

### Sample answer

Situation: In my role as [job title] at [workplace], I noticed that [process/documentation] sometimes had [error or inconsistency]. Task: I wanted to prevent problems and raise the quality of our work without blaming anyone. Action: I double-checked [specific item], told my supervisor what I found, and suggested a simple fix: [checklist, second review, or clearer instructions]. I helped train my teammates on it and tracked results for [time period]. Result: Errors dropped by [amount or description], and the new step became standard practice on our team. I believe excellence comes from careful habits, speaking up early, and being open to feedback.

Question 8

## Tell me about a time you helped someone overcome a barrier to getting the help or service they needed.

What they're asking: Relates to the emphasis on access, meaning helping people reach the care and services they need.

### Sample answer

Situation: At [workplace], a [patient/customer] kept missing [appointments/services] because of [barrier, e.g., transportation, confusing paperwork, or scheduling conflicts]. Task: My goal was to help them get what they needed despite the obstacle. Action: I asked what was getting in the way, then researched options such as [flexible times, community resources, or simplified forms]. I coordinated with [colleague/department], walked them through each step, and confirmed they understood the plan. Result: They [attended/completed the service] and later told us the process felt much easier. That experience taught me to look beyond the obvious problem and ask what's actually stopping someone, then help remove it.

Question 9

## Walk me through your work history and how it prepared you for this position.

What they're asking: Employers review complete work history and minimum qualifications to evaluate experience and credentials.

### Sample answer

Situation: I started my career as [first role] at [employer], where I learned [core skills]. Task: I wanted to build toward a role like this one, so I looked for experiences that would grow my responsibility. Action: I moved into [second role], where I [key responsibilities and achievements], and then [third role], where I [what you led or improved]. I also earned [license, certification, or training] to meet the requirements for roles like this. Result: Together, these jobs gave me [specific skills] and a record of [accomplishment]. Each one lines up with the qualifications listed in this posting, and I've listed every position, including dates, so you can see the full picture of my experience.

Question 10

## Tell me about a time you had to keep up with required training, certifications, or compliance paperwork. How did you stay on top of it?

What they're asking: Relates to the health and immunization readiness and documentation that offers depend on after an interview.

### Sample answer

Situation: In my role at [workplace], I was required to maintain [certification, training, or compliance records] with firm deadlines. Task: I needed to stay current without letting it interfere with my daily responsibilities. Action: I created a tracking sheet with expiration dates, set reminders [number] weeks ahead, and kept digital and paper copies of important records in one place. When I saw a gap, such as [missing document], I contacted [the right person] right away. Result: I was never out of compliance, and a colleague later adopted my tracker. Being organized and proactive with requirements like these helps me start a new role smoothly and keeps patients and coworkers safe.

## How to prepare

- Apply online only, and don't also email, fax, or mail a resume. Check the minimum qualifications on each posting first, because applications can't be edited after submission.

- List your complete work history on the application. At Cheshire Medical Center this can take 30 minutes to an hour, so have dates, employers, and duties ready.

- If you interview at Cheshire Medical Center, arrive at least 15 minutes early and allow extra time because parking can be limited. If you need accommodations for applying or interviewing, request them through talent acquisition.

- Ask the recruiter for the salary and job description before the interview (Cheshire Medical Center), and prepare a few STAR stories that you can adapt to different questions.

- Before the post-offer health screening (DHMC and Clinics), gather a valid photo ID, the completed pre-placement health questionnaire, your immunization records, and any prior TB test results.

## Questions to ask the interviewer

- What would success look like in this role in the first 90 days?

- How does the team communicate and collaborate day to day?

- What are the biggest challenges someone in this position is likely to face?

- What are the next steps in the process, and what timeline should I expect?

# Interview questions at Fidelity Investments | aNewJob

Source: https://anewjob.com/interview-questions/at-fidelity

Interview prep · Companies

# Interview questions at Fidelity Investments

Fidelity Investments says it looks for candidates who can show how they have used their skills in real situations and what value they bring, mostly through behavioral "Tell me about a time..." questions. It also assesses fit with the role, the business's needs and its culture, a clear reason for applying, professionalism, and honesty at every stage. The process varies by role and location, so confirm the details with your recruiter.

## How Fidelity Investments hires

- Application: recruiters compare your resume, skills and answers to any job questions against the job requirements. How fast you hear back depends on how many people applied, and Fidelity says a slow reply is normal.

- Recruiter screening call: a phone conversation (Fidelity says it is not an interview) about your skills, goals and career plans. You confirm the role, location, salary, benefits and expectations. You also learn how many interviews there will be, how long they are, who will interview you, and whether there are skills assessments or case studies.

- Interviews: formal interviews with hiring managers, other employees and/or a panel. Most candidates have at least two rounds, first with recruiters and hiring managers, then with the team. Formats include video (mostly Zoom, sometimes platforms such as HireVue) and in person. Some roles add skills assessments or case studies, and VP-level and senior roles have a more in-depth process that relies more on behavioral interviewing.

- Feedback and next steps: your recruiter explains next steps and timing, or offers coaching. You may get feedback from the hiring manager or panel, and Fidelity also asks candidates for feedback on the process.

- Selection and offer: the hiring manager or panel decides, and the recruiter makes the offer and may help shape it.

- You decide: you weigh the offer, alone or with a partner or family.

The process varies by role and location.

Question 1

## Tell me about yourself and why you applied for this role.

What they're asking: Tests whether you have a clear reason for applying, shown in a concise career summary that matches the role.

### Sample answer

I'm a [current role/background] with [number] years of experience in [field]. Most recently, at [employer], I was responsible for [key responsibility], and I [specific accomplishment with a result, e.g., improved a process or grew a metric]. What I enjoy most is [aspect of the work], and I want to build on that by [goal for the next role]. When I read this job description, I saw a strong match: you need someone who can [requirement 1] and [requirement 2], and I've done both. I also researched the team and the business unit, and the chance to [specific aspect of the role] is exactly the direction I want my career to go. I'd like to bring my skills in [skill] to help the team [business goal].

Question 2

## Why do you want to work for Fidelity?

What they're asking: Tests whether you have researched the company and can connect your motivation to its mission of strengthening the financial well-being of its customers.

### Sample answer

Situation: when I was looking at my next move, I wanted work with a purpose I could explain to my family. Task: I researched the companies I was considering, including Fidelity's website, its stated mission, and [other source, e.g., a conversation with a current or former employee]. Action: I found the mission, to strengthen the financial well-being of customers, matched work I've already cared about, such as [specific example, e.g., helping a client or friend understand their budget]. Result: that experience taught me I do my best work when I can see the impact on a real person's finances. I'd bring that motivation, along with my skills in [skill], to the [role] and learn more about [business unit] from the team.

Question 3

## Tell me about a time you used one of your strengths to achieve a specific result.

What they're asking: Tests whether you describe what you accomplished through your strengths rather than just listing them.

### Sample answer

One of my strengths is [strength, e.g., organization]. Situation: at [employer], our team was facing [problem, e.g., missed deadlines on a recurring report]. Task: I was asked to [your responsibility]. Action: I used my strength in [strength] to [specific steps, e.g., map the workflow, build a shared tracker, and set weekly check-ins]. I kept the team updated and adjusted when [obstacle] came up. Result: we [quantified outcome, e.g., delivered every report on time for the next [number] months and cut rework by [percent]]. What I learned is that a strength only matters when it produces a result others can see, so I now start every project by asking what outcome I'm aiming for.

Question 4

## Describe a time you helped a frustrated or upset customer.

What they're asking: Tests the confidence combined with warmth that customer-facing roles require.

### Sample answer

Situation: at [employer], a customer came to me upset because [issue, e.g., a charge they didn't understand] and had already been waiting a while. Task: I needed to calm the situation and find a real solution. Action: I stayed calm, spoke in a friendly, steady tone, and let them explain fully without interrupting. I apologized for the frustration, then confirmed my understanding of the problem before explaining the options clearly. I [specific step, e.g., looked into the account details and walked them through the fix]. Result: the customer [outcome, e.g., thanked me and stayed with us], and I received [feedback or recognition]. I learned that listening first, then acting confidently, turns most tense conversations around.

Question 5

## Tell me about a mistake you made at work and what you learned from it.

What they're asking: Tests whether you can learn from past successes and mistakes and be honest about them.

### Sample answer

Situation: at [employer], I was handling [task] and I missed [specific error, e.g., a detail in a data entry], which I discovered after [consequence]. Task: I needed to own the error and limit the damage. Action: I told my manager right away rather than hoping nobody noticed, explained what happened, and proposed a fix. I corrected the issue within [timeframe] and told the affected people myself. Then I created [safeguard, e.g., a checklist and a second review step]. Result: the issue was resolved with [outcome], and I haven't repeated the error since. I learned that speaking up quickly protects trust, and that building a simple check into my routine is better than relying on memory.

Question 6

## Tell me about a time you used skills from a previous job, school or activity in a new situation.

What they're asking: Tests whether you can show transferable skills from retail, hospitality, internships, clubs or other experience.

### Sample answer

Situation: I started in [retail/hospitality/school activity], and later took on [new situation, e.g., a project at an internship] where I had little formal experience. Task: I had to [goal] with a quick learning curve. Action: I realized that handling busy shifts at [previous job] had taught me to [skill, e.g., prioritize, communicate clearly and stay composed with customers]. I applied that by [specific steps, e.g., organizing tasks by urgency and checking in with colleagues]. Result: I [outcome, e.g., finished the project on time and received positive feedback from my supervisor]. It showed me that skills aren't tied to one industry. I now look for ways to connect what I've done before to whatever I'm taking on next.

Question 7

## Tell me about a time you took a leadership role, even without a formal title.

What they're asking: Tests leadership evidence from work, clubs, campus roles or internships, and whether you can add value to a team.

### Sample answer

Situation: in [club, internship or job], our group was [challenge, e.g., disorganized ahead of an important event or deadline]. Task: nobody had been assigned to lead, so I offered to coordinate. Action: I split the work based on people's strengths, set a simple schedule, and checked in with each person regularly. When [obstacle] came up, I [specific adjustment]. I also made sure quieter members had a chance to share ideas. Result: we [quantified outcome, e.g., finished two days early and received praise from [stakeholder]]. I learned that leading is mostly about making it easy for others to do their best work, and I'd bring that approach to a team here.

Question 8

## Give an example of when you helped meet an important business need or goal.

What they're asking: Tests fit: whether your skills can help meet business needs and add value.

### Sample answer

Situation: at [employer], our team had a goal to [business goal, e.g., reduce turnaround time or improve customer satisfaction], and we were falling short. Task: I was responsible for [your part]. Action: I reviewed [data or feedback] to find the cause, discovered [insight], and proposed [solution]. I got buy-in from my manager and [colleagues], then implemented the change, tracking results weekly. Result: we [quantified outcome, e.g., improved the metric by [percent] within [timeframe]]. What I learned is to start from the business goal rather than from my own task list. That's the mindset I'd bring to this role: understanding what the team needs to achieve and finding where I can add the most value.

Question 9

## Tell me about a time you disagreed with a colleague or manager. How did you handle it?

What they're asking: Tests professionalism and the ability to work through differences constructively.

### Sample answer

Situation: on a project at [employer], a colleague and I disagreed about [issue, e.g., how to prioritize tasks]. Task: we needed to settle it without hurting the work or our relationship. Action: I asked to talk privately, listened to their reasoning first, and explained mine using facts rather than opinion. We found we shared the goal of [shared goal], so I suggested [compromise or test, e.g., trying their approach for one week and reviewing the results]. Result: we [outcome, e.g., adopted a combined approach], the project finished on schedule, and we worked well together afterward. I learned that assuming good intent and focusing on the shared goal keeps disagreements productive and professional.

Question 10

## Tell me about a time you had to be honest when it would have been easier not to be.

What they're asking: Tests honesty, which candidates are expected to show at every stage of the process.

### Sample answer

Situation: at [employer], I realized that [issue, e.g., a number I had reported to my manager was wrong, or I couldn't meet a deadline I'd promised]. Task: I had to decide whether to quietly work around it or disclose it. Action: I chose to be upfront. I went to [person] the same day, explained exactly what happened, took responsibility, and brought a plan: [specific plan to fix or renegotiate]. Result: [outcome, e.g., they appreciated the early warning, we adjusted the schedule, and the impact was small]. I learned that honest, early communication builds more trust than a perfect record. I apply the same standard in interviews, which is why I only describe experience I've genuinely had.

## How to prepare

- Prepare plenty of stories in advance, and for each one describe the situation, what you did and what you learned. Focus on what you accomplished, not just a list of strengths.

- Know your resume and the job description, and be ready to explain how your background fits the role. Keep your career summary to four sentences or fewer, saying what you bring and what you want to achieve.

- Research Fidelity's culture, history and businesses through its website, social media, LinkedIn, and current or former employees. Ask your recruiter which business unit you will interview with.

- Use your recruiter: raise any mismatches on location, salary or skills early, and mention any conflicts. Treat the interview as a two-way conversation and bring questions about the job.

- For Zoom interviews, choose a quiet, neutral setting, sit down, and dress appropriately for the role. Close strongly by restating your skills and why you are right for the position.

## Questions to ask the interviewer

- What would success look like in this role in the first few months?

- How would you describe the team's working style and how the team collaborates day to day?

- What are the biggest challenges someone in this role would face?

- What are the next steps in the process, and what is the expected timing?

# Interview questions at The Home Depot | aNewJob

Source: https://anewjob.com/interview-questions/at-home-depot

Interview prep · Companies

# Interview questions at The Home Depot

The Home Depot says it looks for people who are eager to learn, good with customers, dependable and adaptable. It also looks for people who show its core values, such as excellent customer service, respect for all people, and doing the right thing. The hiring process varies by role and location, so treat the steps below as a general outline and check your own invitation for details.

## How The Home Depot hires

- Apply online. Every role starts with an application, and The Home Depot only accepts applications on careers.homedepot.com (or careerdepot.homedepot.com for current associates). The same site is used to check your application status. Be wary of anyone posing as the company by text, email or messaging apps, especially if they ask for money.

- Take the online assessment (in-store and distribution center hourly roles). It has 53 questions, can be taken from home, and must be finished within 96 hours of starting. You can stop and restart as often as you like in that time. One set of responses counts for several hourly roles, including Store and MET, so you do not retake it for each application. If you need an accommodation, or a disability could affect your performance, email myTHDHR@homedepot.com.

- Get contacted for an interview if your application is selected. You may hear by email and/or phone.

- Interview at your local store (store roles). A 2018 company newsroom post described a tool that let hourly applicants book their own in-person interviews.

- If you don't hear back after one interview, you can submit a new application for a different store or role (store roles, per the company's 2020 in-store interview tips).

The process varies by role and location.

Question 1

## Tell me about a time you gave excellent customer service.

What they're asking: Excellent Customer Service is a named core value, and the assessment includes a Customer Focus section on how you deal with customers.

### Sample answer

At my [job/volunteer role] at [workplace], a customer came in looking for [product] for a [project]. My goal was to help them succeed, not just point to an aisle. I asked about their budget, space and experience, and realized their first choice wouldn't suit the project. I walked them to a better option, explained how to use it, and made sure all their questions were answered. I also wrote down the key steps so they could refer to them at home. They bought the right product and later came back to tell me the project worked. My [manager/supervisor] mentioned it to the team. It taught me that going the extra mile usually starts with listening.

Question 2

## Tell me about a time you had to learn something new quickly.

What they're asking: This tests the Learning Potential area of the assessment and the eagerness to learn candidates are asked to show.

### Sample answer

When I started at [workplace/school], I had to learn [system/skill/process] within [timeframe], and I had no prior experience with it. I needed to be productive without making costly mistakes. I was upfront with my [manager/teacher] about what I didn't know, asked a experienced coworker to show me the basics, and practiced with [example] during slow periods. I also kept notes and checked my work against them. Within [timeframe] I was handling [task] on my own, and I later helped a new teammate learn it too. I'm comfortable saying 'I don't know yet,' and I treat that as the start of learning, not a weakness.

Question 3

## Describe a time you had to think on your feet or change course on a project.

What they're asking: Adaptability is one of the qualities candidates are asked to show, and the assessment looks at how you handle a changing environment.

### Sample answer

At [workplace/school], I was working on [project] when [unexpected change, e.g., a supplier delay, a new requirement, a teammate out sick] meant our plan no longer worked. I needed to keep us on track with the deadline of [date]. I quickly reviewed what was still possible, proposed a revised plan to my [team/lead], and reassigned tasks so the most urgent work came first. I stayed in touch with everyone as things changed. We finished [on time/with only a small delay], and the result was [outcome]. I learned that staying calm and communicating early makes changing course much easier.

Question 4

## Tell me about a time you faced a tough decision and had to do the right thing.

What they're asking: Doing the Right Thing is a core value that includes good judgment and accepting responsibility for your actions.

### Sample answer

At [workplace], I noticed that [situation, e.g., a pricing error, a skipped safety step, a mistake I made on an order]. Fixing it would take extra time, and nobody would likely have noticed otherwise. I felt responsible for getting it right rather than just getting it done quickly. I told my [supervisor] what had happened, owned my part, and proposed a fix. Then I [corrected the issue/redid the work] and checked it again. It cost me [time], but the problem was resolved before it affected a customer or coworker. My supervisor appreciated the honesty. I'd rather admit a mistake early than hope it goes unnoticed.

Question 5

## How have you given back to your community?

What they're asking: Giving Back is a core value, and candidates are asked to show a willingness to give back.

### Sample answer

I've volunteered with [organization/cause] for [length of time]. Last [season/year], they needed help with [event/project], and I offered to take on [responsibility]. I committed [number] hours, recruited [number] friends or classmates, and organized a simple schedule so everyone knew their role. On the day, I [specific actions, e.g., set up, guided participants, handled supplies]. We [result, e.g., served 200 people, finished the build in a weekend]. I enjoy it because I can see the difference immediately. I'd welcome opportunities to volunteer alongside coworkers, because it builds teamwork as well as helping the community.

Question 6

## Tell me about a time you worked with someone very different from you.

What they're asking: Respect for All People is a core value covering mutual respect and working as one team, free of discrimination and harassment.

### Sample answer

On a [project/shift] at [workplace/school], I was paired with a teammate whose background and working style were quite different from mine. They preferred [style], while I preferred [style], and early on we missed a few handoffs. I wanted us to work well together and respect each other's strengths. I asked them privately how they liked to communicate, shared my own preferences, and we agreed on a quick check-in at [time]. I also asked for their ideas and credited them in front of the team. Our work improved, and we finished [result]. I learned that respect starts with curiosity instead of assumptions.

Question 7

## Tell me about a time you helped a teammate grow, or spoke up with an idea or concern.

What they're asking: Taking Care of Our People covers treating people well, encouraging associates to speak up, and recognizing and developing them.

### Sample answer

At [workplace/school], a newer teammate, [name/a new teammate], was struggling with [task] and hesitant to ask for help. I wanted them to feel supported and succeed. I offered to walk through the task with them, showed them a method that had worked for me, and let them try it while I watched. When they got it right, I made a point of telling our [manager] about their progress. They became confident enough to suggest [improvement], which we adopted. Seeing someone grow was rewarding, and it reminded me that encouragement and recognition make people more willing to speak up.

Question 8

## Describe a time you came up with a creative way to improve something at work or school.

What they're asking: Entrepreneurial Spirit is a core value about finding creative ways to serve customers, improve the business and share best practices.

### Sample answer

At [workplace/school], I noticed that [problem, e.g., customers waited too long, supplies ran out, the same question kept coming up]. I thought we could do better and wanted to try a fix without disrupting anyone. I suggested [idea, e.g., a labeled shelf, a quick checklist, a reorganized schedule] to my [manager], offered to trial it for [timeframe], and tracked the results. It reduced [problem] by [result/estimate]. Once it worked, I explained it to my coworkers and wrote it down so others could use it. Small ideas can make a real difference, and sharing what works helps everyone.

Question 9

## Tell me about a time you were relied on to finish a task reliably and on time.

What they're asking: The Responsibility part of the assessment measures how dependable you are and whether you finish tasks reliably and on time.

### Sample answer

At [workplace/school], I was responsible for [task] that others depended on, with a deadline of [date/time]. Midway through, [obstacle, e.g., a coworker was absent, I had competing priorities] put the deadline at risk. I wanted to deliver as promised. I listed what remained, started with the most important pieces, and told my [manager] early that I might need [help/extra time]. I stayed [extra time/focused] and double-checked my work. I finished [on time] and nothing was missed. My [manager] now trusts me with [responsibility]. Being dependable means doing the work and communicating early when something threatens it.

Question 10

## What makes you unique, and what passions drive you?

What they're asking: Candidates are asked to tell the interviewer what's unique about them and what passions drive them, and to give answers that show their personality and experience.

### Sample answer

I'm someone who [trait, e.g., loves fixing things, enjoys helping people finish projects], and that comes from [background, e.g., helping my family renovate, a hobby, a past job]. At [workplace/school/home], I [specific situation and task, e.g., taught myself to do X so I could Y]. I researched it, practiced on small jobs, and then helped [person] with theirs. The result was [outcome], and I enjoyed explaining the steps so they could do it next time. That mix of hands-on curiosity and wanting to help others is what drives me. I'm also honest about what I don't know, and I enjoy learning the rest.

## How to prepare

- Take the online assessment somewhere free of distractions so you can focus. Answer honestly, and if a question asks how your last manager would describe you, you can think of a project lead or teacher instead.

- Be eager to learn and honest about what you know and don't. Retail or home-improvement experience isn't required, because The Home Depot trains associates.

- Prepare short examples of excellent customer service, a time you adapted, and a time you gave back to your community. Add what makes you unique.

- Arrive at least 15 minutes early, since big stores can be a maze for first-time visitors. Dress your best, but remember it's a casual company where store associates often wear comfortable work clothes.

- Let your personality and experience show, and bring questions to ask. If you need an accommodation for the assessment or interview, email myTHDHR@homedepot.com.

## Questions to ask the interviewer

- What benefits are available from day one?

- How much is teamwork valued on this team?

- How would you describe the company culture here?

- What does a successful first month look like in this role?

# Interview questions at Starbucks | aNewJob

Source: https://anewjob.com/interview-questions/at-starbucks

Interview prep · Companies

# Interview questions at Starbucks

Starbucks says it assesses job-related skills, how well you fit the job description and its required qualifications, and how you show its five values: Craft, Courage, Results, Belonging and Joy. Interviews are behavioral-based, so expect to share specific examples of your impact. The process varies by role and location, so treat this guide as a general roadmap and follow the instructions in your own emails and job posting.

## How Starbucks hires

- Explore opportunities: browse open roles on the Career Hub (coffeehouses, support centers and roasting plants), read job descriptions carefully, turn on job alerts and keep your profile up to date. Retail hourly postings (barista, shift supervisor, shift manager) are refreshed every 90 days, and barista applications are always accepted.

- Apply online: upload a recent resume on the Career Hub. You can apply to several openings and coffeehouses, and you will get an email confirming your application was received.

- Complete Applicant Insights, only if your role requires it: if you meet the basic requirements, you get an email invitation to an online questionnaire of about 20 minutes with no time limit. Finish it within 7 days (reminders come on days 3 and 6) or your application won't move forward. Your responses carry over to other applications for the same job for 90 days.

- Stay connected: check your status on the Career Hub. If you are selected, a recruiter or coffeehouse leader reaches out to schedule next steps. If you aren't moving forward after the initial resume review, you are told by email.

- Interview: this step applies to all roles and is behavioral-based. If you need an accommodation during the interview process, contact applicantaccommodation@starbucks.com or call 1-888-611-2258.

- Get started, if selected: new employees get essential training in their first month, with more at 90 and 190 days.

The process varies by role and location.

Question 1

## Tell me about a time you learned a new skill quickly, or taught one to someone else.

What they're asking: This tests the Craft value, which covers learning and teaching in the pursuit of growth.

### Sample answer

At [previous job/school], my team switched to [new system/process], and I had a week to learn it before we went live. I knew a mistake could slow everyone down, so I wanted to be ready and help others too. I practiced the basics each morning, wrote myself a one-page cheat sheet, and asked [coworker/manager] to check my work. Once I felt confident, I offered to show two newer teammates the steps and shared my cheat sheet. By launch day, our team finished [task] with [specific result, e.g., no errors in the first week]. I learned that teaching what I know also helps me remember it, and I'd bring that habit to this role.

Question 2

## Describe a time when paying close attention to detail made a real difference.

What they're asking: This tests the Craft value of delighting in the rigor of the details, and how your skills fit the role.

### Sample answer

In my role at [workplace], I was responsible for [task, e.g., preparing orders/stocking/checking records]. During a busy [day/shift], I noticed that [specific detail, e.g., a label, quantity or instruction] didn't match what we normally did. I could have kept moving because we were behind, but I knew a small error could affect [customer/team]. I stopped, double-checked it against [source], and corrected it before it went out. I then suggested a quick checklist so we could catch the same issue in future. As a result, [specific outcome, e.g., errors dropped, a customer avoided a problem]. I like doing small things carefully because they add up to a better experience for everyone.

Question 3

## Tell me about a difficult conversation you had to have. How did you handle it?

What they're asking: This tests the Courage value, which includes having difficult conversations with respect.

### Sample answer

At [workplace/school], a teammate, [first name or 'a coworker'], was regularly arriving late, and the rest of us were covering [task]. I felt the issue needed to be addressed before resentment built up. I asked to talk privately and started by saying I valued working with them. I described what I'd seen, without blame, and asked if something was going on. They shared that [reason, e.g., a schedule conflict], and together we agreed on [solution, e.g., swapping shifts or giving earlier notice]. Within [timeframe], the lateness stopped and our working relationship improved. I learned that speaking up early and respectfully usually works better than staying quiet.

Question 4

## Give me an example of a time you pursued a bold idea outside your comfort zone.

What they're asking: This tests the Courage value of pursuing bold ideas beyond your comfort zone.

### Sample answer

At [workplace/organization], I noticed that [problem, e.g., long waits, low turnout, messy handoffs]. I had an idea to [bold idea], but I'd never led anything like it and was nervous about proposing it. I put together a short plan, asked [manager/teacher] for a chance to test it for [timeframe], and volunteered to do the extra work myself. Not everything went smoothly; [small challenge], so I adjusted by [change]. In the end, [specific result, e.g., wait times fell by X%, attendance rose]. Even though I was uncomfortable, I'm glad I tried. It showed me that a well-prepared idea is worth sharing.

Question 5

## Tell me about a goal you set and consistently achieved. What did you do to stay on track?

What they're asking: This tests the Results value: consistently achieving goals with focus, integrity and drive.

### Sample answer

In my role at [workplace], my goal was to [specific goal, e.g., keep accuracy above X%, reach X sales, finish X tasks per shift] every week for [timeframe]. I knew it would take steady effort rather than one big push. I broke the goal into daily targets, tracked my progress in [tool/notebook], and reviewed it with [manager] each week. When I fell short on [day/week], I was honest about why and adjusted by [change, e.g., reorganizing my routine]. By the end, I hit the goal [number] weeks in a row and [additional outcome]. I stay motivated by measuring progress and being straightforward about what isn't working.

Question 6

## Describe a time you improved a process or tried a new approach that made things work better.

What they're asking: This tests the Results value of continuously innovating, using examples of your impact.

### Sample answer

At [workplace/school], [task/process] was taking longer than it should, and it was frustrating for [team/customers]. I wanted to find a simpler way. I watched where things slowed down and saw that [specific bottleneck]. I suggested [change, e.g., reorganizing the layout, creating a template, splitting the steps], and my [manager/teammates] agreed to try it for [timeframe]. I tracked the results and shared feedback with the group. The change [specific result with numbers, e.g., cut the time by X minutes, reduced errors by X%]. I enjoy finding small improvements, and I always check with the people doing the work before making changes.

Question 7

## Tell me about a time you listened carefully to someone and it changed how you helped them.

What they're asking: This tests the Belonging value of actively listening and connecting with warmth and transparency.

### Sample answer

While working at [workplace], a [customer/classmate/coworker] came to me clearly frustrated about [issue]. At first I started offering a quick solution, but I realized I hadn't actually understood the problem. So I stopped, made eye contact, and let them finish. I then repeated back what I heard to make sure I understood. It turned out their main concern was [real concern], not what I first assumed. I explained honestly what I could and couldn't do, and offered [solution]. They thanked me, and [positive outcome, e.g., stayed as a regular customer, the issue was resolved]. That experience reminded me to listen fully before trying to fix things.

Question 8

## Tell me about a time you helped someone feel included or recognized for who they are.

What they're asking: This tests the Belonging value of recognizing every person for who they are.

### Sample answer

On my [team/class/volunteer group] at [place], a new member, [first name or 'a new teammate'], was sitting quietly at the edges and rarely spoke. I remembered how that felt when I was new, so I wanted to help. I invited them to join me for [activity/break], asked about their background and interests, and learned they were great at [skill]. I then suggested to [leader] that they help with [task related to skill]. They did a great job, and the group noticed. Over the next [timeframe], they became more confident and started sharing ideas. I believe small, genuine gestures can help people feel they belong.

Question 9

## Describe a time you took real pride in your work, even when it was a hectic or difficult day.

What they're asking: This tests the Joy value of taking pride in your work and having fun doing it.

### Sample answer

During a very busy [day/event/season] at [workplace], we were short-staffed and everyone was feeling the pressure. My responsibility was [task], and I wanted to do it well regardless of the stress. I kept my focus on one task at a time, stayed friendly with [customers/teammates], and made a joke or two to keep the mood light. When [problem occurred], I jumped in to help rather than waiting to be asked. At the end of the day, [positive result, e.g., a customer complimented us, we met our targets]. I felt proud because I'd done a good job and helped the people around me enjoy a tough day a bit more.

Question 10

## Tell me about a time you celebrated a teammate's success or a group win.

What they're asking: This tests the Joy value of celebrating each other and your wins, and shows how you work with a team.

### Sample answer

On my team at [workplace/school], [teammate] had been working hard on [goal/project], and the rest of us knew how much effort it took. When they finally [achieved result], I wanted to make sure it didn't pass unnoticed. I checked with [manager/group] and arranged a quick shout-out at [meeting/end of shift], and I brought [small gesture, e.g., a handwritten card, a treat] from the whole team. I also made sure to mention the specific things they did well. The teammate was clearly touched, and the group felt more motivated afterward; [positive result, e.g., we hit our next target]. I think celebrating wins keeps a team close and energized.

## How to prepare

- Think about your strengths, areas to grow, skills and experience, and connect each one to the job description and the required qualifications.

- Prepare a strong introduction covering who you are, your experience, your goals and the value you bring, plus 3 to 5 thoughtful questions for the interviewer.

- Get familiar with behavioral-based interviewing and prepare specific examples of your impact that show the role's competencies and the values of Craft, Courage, Results, Belonging and Joy.

- If your role requires Applicant Insights, try to finish it in one sitting within 7 days, and complete the whole process for one job before applying to another posting for the same job.

- After the interview, send a thank-you note within 48 hours to the hiring manager (or to the recruiter to pass along), reply promptly to follow-ups, and reflect on what went well and what you could prepare better.

## Questions to ask the interviewer

- What does success look like in this role in the first few months?

- What would a typical day or week look like for someone in this position?

- How does the team work together and support each other when things get busy?

- What are the next steps in the process, and when can I expect to hear back?

# Interview questions at Target | aNewJob

Source: https://anewjob.com/interview-questions/at-target

Interview prep · Companies

# Interview questions at Target

Target says it assesses job knowledge, inclusivity, problem-solving, connection and drive, along with its values of Care, Grow and Win. It tells candidates to tie each answer to the skills and values the question asks about, and it calls being genuine your greatest strength. The process varies by role and location, so treat this guide as a general framework and check your own invitation and emails for specifics.

## How Target hires

- Apply online. Every application, whether for stores, supply chain and distribution centers, or corporate roles, goes through Target's Workday system, starting from the job search on Target's careers site. Details vary by role and location.

- Recruiting review. Target's recruitment team reviews your application.

- Interview. The format depends on the role and can be by phone, virtual, in person, or a recorded video interview. Only some business areas use recorded video.

- Recorded video interview (only where used). Within 2 hours of being invited, you get an email from 'Target Careers' (sent from interviews@hirevue.com) with instructions and a unique link. You can practice, then record answers to a series of questions. Plan for about 30 minutes.

- Video review (recorded video candidates). A recruiter or hiring manager watches your answers, reviews your resume and application, and gets back to you with next steps within five business days. If it has been more than ten days, contact your recruiter or the store's HR.

- Offer. It is sent by email, or by phone and email for some recruiter-led candidates. You accept the offer and complete pre-hire screening in your Workday Candidate Homepage.

- Onboarding. This includes the Target Welcome orientation, followed by training.

The process varies by role and location.

Question 1

## Tell me about yourself and why you want this role.

What they're asking: This tests job knowledge: the background that prepared you for the job and why you want it.

### Sample answer

I've spent [X years] in [field or role], most recently as [job title] at [employer]. In that job, [situation: a busy period or challenge], and I was responsible for [task]. I [action: what you did, such as organizing the workload, learning a new system or helping teammates], and as a result [outcome with a number or concrete result if you can]. That experience taught me [skill], which is exactly what this [role title] needs. I want this job because [genuine reason, such as enjoying helping people, liking fast-paced work or wanting to build a career in this area]. I've also read the job description closely, and I'm excited about [specific responsibility].

Question 2

## What training or experience has prepared you for this job, and which of your skills are most relevant?

What they're asking: This checks job knowledge, including your prior work, training and relevant skills.

### Sample answer

The most relevant preparation I have is [experience or training]. In that role, I was expected to [situation and task, such as handle customer questions, move product accurately or manage reports]. I took ownership by [action: a specific routine, tool or habit], and I also completed [training or certification, if any]. The result was [outcome, such as fewer errors, faster turnaround or positive feedback from a manager]. From that, my strongest skills are [skill 1], [skill 2] and [skill 3], and I've seen how each one applies to this job's day-to-day duties, like [duty from the job description]. I'm also eager to learn the parts I haven't done before.

Question 3

## Tell me about a time you worked with someone who thought very differently from you.

What they're asking: This tests inclusivity: working with people who think differently and respecting other points of view.

### Sample answer

On a project at [employer], I was paired with [colleague], who preferred a very different approach to [task]. I wanted to move quickly, while they wanted to plan every step. My task was to make sure we delivered [goal] together. I asked them to explain their reasoning and listened without interrupting, and I realized their planning would prevent [specific problem]. We agreed to plan the first stage carefully and then work faster on the rest. The result was that we finished [on time or early], and the quality was better than either of us would have managed alone. I learned that different perspectives often make the outcome stronger, and I now ask for them early.

Question 4

## Describe a time you faced a challenge at work. How did you assess it and what steps did you take to solve it?

What they're asking: This tests problem-solving: how you assess a challenge, find ways forward and the steps you took.

### Sample answer

At [employer], [situation: for example, a recurring delay, a shortage or a customer complaint] was causing [impact]. My task was to fix it before [deadline or event]. First, I gathered facts by [talking to teammates, checking records or observing the process] and found that the root cause was [cause]. I listed two or three options, weighed the time and effort of each, and chose [solution]. I then [steps you took, including who you told and how you checked it worked]. The result was [measurable or clear outcome]. Afterward I documented what I'd done so the team could use it again, and I now check for root causes before jumping to a quick fix.

Question 5

## Give an example of how you built a strong working relationship with a teammate, manager or customer.

What they're asking: This tests connection: how you partner and communicate with others and what collaboration looks like for you.

### Sample answer

When I started as [role] at [employer], I had to work closely with [person or team], and communication was initially hit-or-miss. My goal was to build a reliable working relationship so we could meet [shared goal]. I set up a quick [daily or weekly] check-in, asked how they preferred to receive updates, and made a point of sharing information early, including when something went wrong. I also offered help when their workload was heavy. Within [timeframe], we were sharing information easily, and the result was [outcome, such as fewer misunderstandings or faster completion]. To me, collaboration means being dependable, communicating clearly and making it easy for others to work with me.

Question 6

## Tell me about a time you made sure your work had real impact. How do you define success on a task or project?

What they're asking: This tests drive: how you make sure your work has impact and how you define success.

### Sample answer

At [employer], I was given [task or project] with the goal of [objective]. I defined success as [specific measure, such as accuracy, customer satisfaction or meeting a deadline], not just finishing the task. To get there, I [actions: broke the work into steps, tracked progress and checked in with the people affected]. Midway, I noticed [issue] and adjusted by [change]. The result was [outcome, ideally with a number or concrete example], and [person] told me it made a difference to [impact]. I like to define success before I start, so I know what I'm aiming for and can tell whether my work is truly helping.

Question 7

## Tell me about a time you put people first and showed up for a teammate or customer.

What they're asking: This connects to the Care value: showing up for each other, making people the priority and treating each other with respect.

### Sample answer

One day at [employer], a teammate, [name or 'a colleague'], was clearly overwhelmed with [situation, such as a heavy workload or a personal difficulty]. Meanwhile, we had [deadline or busy period]. My task was to keep my own work on track while making sure they weren't left struggling. I quietly asked how they were doing, offered to take over [specific task], and let our manager know so we could rebalance the workload without singling them out. The result was that we met our goals, and my teammate later said the support meant a lot. For me, caring means noticing people, acting with respect and being willing to step in.

Question 8

## Describe a time you helped someone grow, or took the initiative to develop your own skills.

What they're asking: This connects to the Grow value: investing in people, focusing on development and creating opportunities to reach full potential.

### Sample answer

At [employer], a new teammate, [name or 'a new hire'], was struggling with [skill or task]. I wanted to help them become confident, and my task was to get them working independently within [timeframe]. I broke the task into small steps, demonstrated it once, watched them try it and gave specific, friendly feedback. I also pointed them to [resource or person]. Within [timeframe], they were handling it alone, and the result was [outcome, such as fewer errors or taking on new tasks]. Teaching also improved my own skills in [area]. I enjoy both learning and helping others develop, because I believe everyone does better when they have room to grow.

Question 9

## Tell me about a time you did the right thing even though it was difficult, or succeeded as part of a team.

What they're asking: This connects to the Win value: doing the right thing, winning the right way and succeeding as part of a team.

### Sample answer

Our team at [employer] was under pressure to hit [goal or deadline], and I noticed that [shortcut or error, such as skipping a check or a mistake in my own work] could have helped us finish sooner but would have caused [problem]. My task was to decide what to do. I told my manager about it right away, explained the risk and suggested [alternative]. I then worked with teammates to split up the extra work. We [action] and finished [outcome], with the work done correctly. It took more effort, but the result was a better outcome and a team that trusted each other. I'd rather win the right way than take a shortcut.

Question 10

## Tell me about a time you listened to a point of view that differed from yours and changed your approach.

What they're asking: This tests inclusivity: listening to others, respecting other points of view and keeping things fair.

### Sample answer

While working on [project or task] at [employer], I was confident about [approach], but a teammate, [name or 'a colleague'], disagreed and raised a concern I hadn't considered: [concern]. My task was to decide whether to stick with my plan or adjust it, while keeping the discussion respectful. I asked questions until I understood their view, then checked the facts with [source or person]. It turned out they were right about [point], so I changed [specific part of the plan] and thanked them for speaking up. The result was [outcome, such as avoiding a mistake or a better result]. Since then, I actively invite others to challenge my thinking, because fair decisions come from hearing everyone.

## How to prepare

- Review the job description and research the company and the role, so you can speak to your qualifications and show how the job fits your career goals.

- Practice answers about your experience and skills, keep each one to about five minutes, and tie it to the skills and values the question asks about.

- For virtual or recorded interviews, test your technology, use a well-lit and quiet space, check what is visible behind you, and practice on camera. For recorded video, use the unlimited practice question and watch the introduction video all the way through, because it can't be replayed.

- Answer from your own knowledge and experience. AI tools are not allowed unless they are an approved accommodation or assistive technology, and accommodation requests can go to candidate.accommodations@HRHelp.Target.com or to your recruiter.

- Be yourself, and remember you are interviewing Target too. Afterward, thank the interviewer and confirm next steps. If you don't get an offer, ask about other openings that fit your skills and set up job alerts.

## Questions to ask the interviewer

- What would success look like in this role in the first few months?

- How does the team usually collaborate and communicate day to day?

- What opportunities are there to learn and develop in this role?

- What are the next steps, and when can I expect to hear back?

# Interview questions at UPS | aNewJob

Source: https://anewjob.com/interview-questions/at-ups

Interview prep · Companies

# Interview questions at UPS

UPS describes its values as Integrity, Safety and Wellness, Service, Teamwork, Excellence, Innovation and Sustainability, and says mutual respect and mindfulness run through its culture. It also lists concrete requirements for particular jobs, such as physical stamina for warehouse work and driving skills for delivery drivers. The hiring process varies by role and location, so treat this guide as a general map and follow the instructions you get from UPS for your own application.

## How UPS hires

- Warehouse workers / package handlers: fill out an application and watch a short video about what the job is like.

- Warehouse workers / package handlers: you could get an offer and schedule your first day in under 10 minutes. UPS advertises 'No Interview Needed' for some positions, and its FAQ says the application process has no interview step. If an interview is needed, UPS tells you by phone, email or text.

- Warehouse workers / package handlers: go to your hiring appointment. You get email and text reminders and can reschedule through your application link. Then check your email to confirm your official start date and read the welcome letter.

- Warehouse workers / package handlers: before day one, submit proof of identity and employment eligibility online. Bring original documents (one List A document, or one List B plus one List C). Copies are not accepted.

- Warehouse workers / package handlers: arrive on day one ready to finish any remaining onboarding steps.

- Package delivery drivers (and warehouse worker/cover drivers): fill out an application and watch a short video.

- Package delivery drivers: if you get an offer, schedule and complete a UPS road test and a DOT physical. Your driving record is reviewed as part of the background check.

- Package delivery drivers: complete the training materials sent by email (an online pre-course you must pass before in-person training) and submit proof of identity and employment eligibility online.

- Package delivery drivers: memorize the 5 Seeing Habits and the 10-Point Commentary. Then attend the required multi-day Driver Training at a designated facility, where you show both verbal knowledge and behind-the-wheel skills.

- Package delivery drivers: receive your uniform, then return to your assigned center for hands-on instruction and coaching.

- Tractor-trailer drivers: apply and watch a short video. If you get an offer, schedule the road test and DOT physical, pass a drug screen, submit proof of identity and employment eligibility online, and receive a uniform.

- Professional/corporate roles: apply online (uploading a resume fills in some fields automatically). If selected, you start the interview process. Select technical roles also take a skills assessment. Then you receive an offer and begin onboarding.

The process varies by role and location.

Question 1

## Tell me about a time you did the right thing even though it was hard.

What they're asking: Integrity is a named UPS value, described as doing what is right even when it is hard.

### Sample answer

Situation: In my role at [employer], I noticed a coworker had scanned [items/records] as complete when they weren't, and I knew correcting it would make our team's numbers look worse that day. Task: I needed to make sure the information was accurate without simply blaming someone. Action: I spoke with my coworker privately first, explained the problem, and then told our supervisor so the records could be fixed. I offered to help redo the work. Result: We corrected it before it caused [problem], my supervisor thanked me for being upfront, and my coworker and I agreed on a double-check habit. It wasn't comfortable, but honesty protected the customer and our team's credibility.

Question 2

## Describe a time you spotted a safety risk. What did you do?

What they're asking: Safety and Wellness is a named UPS value, covering looking after yourself and each other.

### Sample answer

Situation: While working at [workplace], I noticed [a spill/a box stacked unsteadily/a blocked walkway] near a busy area. Task: I wanted to prevent anyone from getting hurt, even though it wasn't strictly my assigned area. Action: I stopped what I was doing, put up a [cone/warning] and told people nearby to go around. Then I reported it to my supervisor right away and stayed until it was cleaned up or secured. Afterward I suggested we check that area at the start of each shift. Result: Nobody was hurt, the hazard was fixed within [timeframe], and the team adopted the quick check. I learned that small actions in the moment protect everyone.

Question 3

## Tell me about a time you put a customer's needs first.

What they're asking: Service, meaning putting customers first, is a named UPS value.

### Sample answer

Situation: At [employer], a customer came in upset because [their order was late/incorrect] and they needed it by [deadline]. Task: I needed to solve the problem and keep their trust, even though the delay wasn't my fault. Action: I listened without interrupting, apologized for the inconvenience, and checked what options we had. I then arranged [a replacement/faster option] and followed up to confirm it arrived. I also told my team what went wrong so we could avoid repeating it. Result: The customer received what they needed on time, thanked me, and continued to [shop with us/use our service]. It showed me that following through matters as much as the first apology.

Question 4

## Give an example of how you contributed to a team reaching a shared goal.

What they're asking: Teamwork, described as people working together toward shared success, is a named UPS value.

### Sample answer

Situation: My team at [employer] had to finish [a large task/project] by [deadline], and we were behind because [reason]. Task: I wanted to help us finish together rather than just complete my own part. Action: I finished my section early, then asked teammates where they were stuck. I took on [specific task], and we reorganized so people worked on what they did best. I also checked in with the group at [interval] so nobody was surprised. Result: We finished [on time/ahead of schedule], and the team lead noted how well we coordinated. I learned that offering help early often matters more than doing my own job perfectly.

Question 5

## This job is physically demanding. Tell me about a time you kept up a high level of effort over a long shift.

What they're asking: UPS describes warehouse and package handler work as very physical, needing stamina around conveyor belts and large machinery.

### Sample answer

Situation: At [previous job/activity], I regularly worked [number]-hour shifts that involved [lifting, standing, moving quickly], often in [hot/cold/busy conditions]. Task: I needed to stay productive and safe through the whole shift, not just the first few hours. Action: I paced myself, used proper lifting technique, took my scheduled breaks to drink water and eat, and wore [appropriate footwear/layers]. I also watched my surroundings carefully when equipment was moving nearby. Result: I kept my pace and accuracy to the end of each shift, had no injuries, and [my supervisor relied on me during peak periods]. I'm confident I can handle physical work by preparing well and staying focused.

Question 6

## Tell me about a time you went beyond what was expected of you.

What they're asking: Excellence is a named UPS value, with the aim of exceeding expectations.

### Sample answer

Situation: At [employer], I was responsible for [routine task], and I noticed customers and coworkers often had to [ask for the same information/redo steps]. Task: My job was only to complete the task, but I wanted to make the result better. Action: On my own time between tasks, I created [a checklist/labeled system/quick guide], tested it for a week, and asked my supervisor for feedback before sharing it. Result: Errors dropped by [amount or 'noticeably'], new teammates learned the task faster, and my supervisor asked me to help train others. Doing a bit more than required made the whole team more reliable.

Question 7

## Describe a time you came up with a new idea or solved a problem in a new way.

What they're asking: Innovation, described as being trusted problem solvers and embracing new ideas, is a named UPS value.

### Sample answer

Situation: At [employer], we kept running into [recurring problem, such as delays or mix-ups] during [busy period]. Task: I wanted to find a fix that didn't require extra resources. Action: I looked at where the problem started, and I suggested [new approach] to my supervisor. We tried it for [timeframe] and I tracked the results. When part of it didn't work, I adjusted it based on teammates' feedback. Result: The problem decreased by [amount or 'significantly'], and the new method became our standard routine. I enjoy trying new approaches, and I'm just as happy to learn a better way someone else has found.

Question 8

## Tell me about a time you helped reduce waste or contributed to your community.

What they're asking: Sustainability, described as reducing environmental impact and working with communities, is a named UPS value.

### Sample answer

Situation: At [workplace/school/organization], I noticed we were throwing away [materials/usable supplies] regularly. Task: I wanted to cut that waste and involve others rather than just changing my own habits. Action: I proposed [recycling/reusing/donating] those items, set up clearly labeled bins, and explained the plan briefly at a team meeting. I also arranged to donate [items] to [local organization]. Result: Within [timeframe], we cut [type of waste] noticeably, and the local organization benefitted from [donation]. My coworkers kept it going after I stopped leading it. It taught me that simple, practical steps can help both the environment and the community.

Question 9

## Tell me about a disagreement with a coworker and how you handled it.

What they're asking: UPS describes mutual respect and mindfulness as permeating its culture, and teamwork as a value.

### Sample answer

Situation: At [employer], a coworker and I disagreed about how to divide [tasks/schedule] during a busy week, and the tension was affecting the team. Task: I needed to settle it respectfully so we could keep working well together. Action: I asked to talk privately, listened to their concerns first, and explained my view calmly without blaming. We found that they were worried about [concern], so we agreed on [compromise], and I checked in a few days later to see whether it was working. Result: We completed the work smoothly, the tension disappeared, and we worked together well afterward. I try to assume good intentions and talk directly.

Question 10

## Tell me about a time you had to learn a detailed procedure and prove you could do it correctly.

What they're asking: Delivery drivers must memorize set procedures and show both verbal knowledge and behind-the-wheel skills in training; this question also suits any role with onboarding.

### Sample answer

Situation: When I started at [employer/school], I had to learn [detailed procedure, such as safety steps or equipment operation] and be tested on it. Task: I had to memorize the steps and also demonstrate them correctly in practice. Action: I made notes, practiced out loud with [a friend/family member] until I could explain each step without looking, and then practiced doing it hands-on whenever I could. I asked my trainer questions about the parts I got wrong. Result: I passed [the evaluation] on [first attempt/second attempt] and was later asked to help newer people learn it. Preparing before training began made a real difference.

## How to prepare

- Bring original identity and work-eligibility documents (one List A document, or one List B plus one List C) to onboarding. Copies are not accepted.

- For package handler work, dress in layers and wear shoes with sturdy uppers and non-slip soles (no sneakers, loafers or sandals). Bring water because the work is physically demanding.

- Arrive on time every day and line up reliable transportation before your start date.

- If you're going for a driving role, finish the online pre-course and memorize the 5 Seeing Habits and the 10-Point Commentary before in-person Driver Training.

- For professional roles, upload your resume to fill in parts of the application automatically. Prepare a few STAR stories you can adapt to different questions, and report any suspected hiring fraud.

## Questions to ask the interviewer

- What does a typical first week look like in this role?

- What training or coaching will I receive, and who can I go to with questions?

- What qualities do your strongest team members share?

- What are the next steps, and when should I expect to hear back?
