# Technical Skills for Your Resume: A Complete Guide

In today's digital workplace, showcasing the right technical skills on your resume can make the difference between landing an interview and getting overlooked. Whether you're a recent graduate or seasoned professional, understanding how to effectively present your computer skills and software expertise is crucial for career success.

## In This Article

- Understanding Different Types of Technical Skills

- How to List Technical Skills on Your Resume

- Demonstrating Technical Skills Through Work Experience

- Staying Current and Building New Technical Skills

- Key Takeaways

- FAQ

## Understanding Different Types of Technical Skills

Technical skills encompass a broad range of abilities that involve using technology, software, and digital tools to perform job-related tasks. These can be categorized into several key areas: computer skills (operating systems, hardware troubleshooting), software skills (Microsoft Office, Adobe Creative Suite, CRM platforms), programming languages (Python, JavaScript, SQL), and industry-specific tools (AutoCAD for engineering, Salesforce for sales). When identifying your technical skills, consider both hard skills you've learned through formal training and those you've developed through hands-on experience. Don't overlook basic computer skills that might seem obvious to you—many employers still value proficiency in fundamental software like spreadsheet applications, email platforms, and file management systems. The key is matching your technical abilities to what employers in your target field actually need and use daily.

## How to List Technical Skills on Your Resume

The placement and formatting of your technical skills section can significantly impact how recruiters perceive your qualifications. Create a dedicated 'Technical Skills' or 'Core Competencies' section, typically positioned after your professional summary but before your work experience. Use clear categories to organize your skills, such as 'Programming Languages,' 'Software Applications,' or 'Digital Marketing Tools.' List your skills in order of proficiency and relevance to the target position. Instead of simply listing software names, consider adding proficiency levels (Advanced, Intermediate, Basic) or years of experience. For example: 'Microsoft Excel (Advanced, 5+ years)' or 'Python Programming (Intermediate).' This approach gives employers a clearer picture of your actual capabilities rather than just familiarity with various tools. Avoid overwhelming recruiters with an exhaustive list of every program you've ever used. Focus on 8-12 of your strongest, most relevant technical skills that align with the job requirements. Remember that anything you list should be something you're comfortable discussing in detail during an interview.

## Demonstrating Technical Skills Through Work Experience

While a dedicated skills section is important, the most powerful way to showcase your technical abilities is by integrating them into your work experience descriptions. Use specific examples that demonstrate how you've applied these skills to achieve measurable results. Instead of simply stating 'Proficient in Excel,' write 'Utilized advanced Excel functions including pivot tables and VLOOKUP to analyze sales data, resulting in 15% improvement in forecasting accuracy.' Quantify your technical achievements whenever possible. Did your database optimization reduce processing time? Did your social media management software help increase engagement? These concrete examples prove your technical competency while showing the business value you can provide. Action verbs like 'developed,' 'implemented,' 'optimized,' and 'automated' help emphasize your hands-on technical experience. For career changers or recent graduates with limited professional experience, consider including relevant projects, coursework, or volunteer work where you've applied technical skills. A computer science student might describe a coding project, while a marketing graduate could highlight their experience with analytics tools during an internship.

## Staying Current and Building New Technical Skills

Technology evolves rapidly, making continuous learning essential for maintaining relevant technical skills. Regularly research job postings in your field to identify emerging software requirements and trending technologies. Many employers now seek candidates familiar with cloud platforms (AWS, Google Cloud), collaboration tools (Slack, Microsoft Teams), and data analysis software (Tableau, Power BI). Take advantage of free and low-cost learning resources to expand your technical skill set. Platforms like Coursera, LinkedIn Learning, and YouTube offer tutorials on virtually every software application and programming language. Many software companies also provide free training materials and certification programs for their products. Consider pursuing industry-recognized certifications in relevant technologies, as these credentials can significantly strengthen your resume. Don't neglect soft skills that complement your technical abilities. Problem-solving, attention to detail, and the ability to learn new systems quickly are highly valued by employers. When describing your technical skills, weave in these complementary abilities to present yourself as a well-rounded candidate who can both master technology and work effectively with others.

## Key Takeaways

- Organize technical skills into clear categories and list them in order of proficiency and relevance to your target role

- Integrate technical skills into work experience descriptions with specific examples and measurable results

- Focus on 8-12 of your strongest technical skills rather than creating an overwhelming comprehensive list

- Stay current with industry trends and continuously develop new technical skills through online learning platforms

- Include proficiency levels or years of experience to give employers a clearer picture of your actual capabilities

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Should I include basic computer skills like Microsoft Word on my resume?

Include basic computer skills only if they're specifically mentioned in the job posting or if you're applying for entry-level positions. For most professional roles, focus on more advanced or specialized software skills that set you apart from other candidates.

### How do I list technical skills if I'm self-taught?

Self-taught technical skills are absolutely valuable and should be included on your resume. Focus on demonstrating your proficiency through specific projects, results achieved, or certifications earned rather than emphasizing the learning method.

### What if I don't have many technical skills for my desired field?

Research the most important technical skills for your target role and begin learning them through free online resources. Start with the most fundamental tools used in your industry, and consider taking on volunteer projects or freelance work to gain practical experience.

# Transferable Skills: Highlight What Matters Most | aNewJob.com

Source: https://anewjob.com/resume-guide/transferable-skills-resume

# Transferable Skills: Highlight What Matters Most

In today's rapidly evolving job market, the ability to effectively communicate your transferable skills can be the difference between landing your dream job and getting lost in a sea of applicants. Whether you're changing careers, re-entering the workforce, or transitioning from military service to civilian employment, your transferable skills are the golden thread that connects your past experiences to your future opportunities. These versatile abilities—from leadership and problem-solving to communication and project management—transcend industry boundaries and demonstrate your value to potential employers. Understanding how to identify, articulate, and strategically highlight these skills on your resume isn't just important—it's essential for career success in an increasingly competitive landscape.

## In This Article

- Understanding What Makes Skills Transferable

- Strategic Skill Mapping for Your Target Role

- Crafting Compelling Skill-Based Resume Content

- Addressing Skill Gaps and Building Credibility

- Key Takeaways

- FAQ

## Understanding What Makes Skills Transferable

Transferable skills are abilities and competencies that remain valuable across different roles, industries, and career paths. Unlike technical skills that are job-specific, transferable skills represent the fundamental capabilities that make you effective in any professional environment. These fall into three main categories: people skills (communication, teamwork, leadership), thinking skills (problem-solving, critical thinking, creativity), and personal qualities (adaptability, work ethic, time management). The key to leveraging these skills lies in recognizing them within your existing experience. For example, if you've managed a household budget, you've demonstrated financial planning and analytical skills. If you've volunteered for community events, you've shown project coordination and interpersonal abilities. Even seemingly unrelated experiences like coaching youth sports translate to leadership, mentoring, and performance management skills that employers value. The most successful job seekers learn to view their entire life experience through the lens of skill development, identifying patterns of competency that span across their personal, academic, and professional history.

## Strategic Skill Mapping for Your Target Role

Before highlighting transferable skills on your resume, conduct a thorough analysis of your target position and industry. Start by carefully reading job descriptions for roles you're interested in, noting recurring requirements and preferred qualifications. Create a skills inventory by listing all your experiences—paid work, volunteer activities, education, hobbies, and personal projects—then identify the skills demonstrated in each. Next, map your skills to the employer's needs using their language. If a job posting mentions 'stakeholder management,' and you've coordinated between different parent groups for school events, you've demonstrated stakeholder management skills. Use a three-column approach: your experience, the skill it demonstrates, and how it applies to the target role. For career changers, focus on leadership experiences, process improvements you've implemented, or cross-functional collaboration. Military veterans should translate military terminology into civilian business language—'led a squad of 12' becomes 'managed a team of 12 direct reports.' This strategic mapping ensures your resume speaks directly to what employers are seeking while authentically representing your capabilities.

## Crafting Compelling Skill-Based Resume Content

Transform your transferable skills into compelling resume content by using the CAR method: Context, Action, and Result. Instead of simply listing 'communication skills,' provide specific examples that demonstrate impact. For instance: 'Facilitated weekly cross-departmental meetings with 15+ stakeholders, resulting in 30% faster project completion times and improved team collaboration.' Start each bullet point with strong action verbs that convey leadership and initiative: 'spearheaded,' 'orchestrated,' 'streamlined,' or 'championed.' Quantify your achievements whenever possible—numbers provide concrete evidence of your capabilities. If you increased efficiency, managed budgets, led teams, or improved processes, include specific metrics. For those with limited traditional work experience, draw from academic projects, volunteer work, or personal initiatives. A college student who organized fundraising events can highlight project management, budget oversight, and relationship building. Create a dedicated 'Core Competencies' or 'Key Skills' section near the top of your resume, featuring 8-12 transferable skills most relevant to your target role. This section serves as a quick reference for hiring managers and helps your resume pass through Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) that scan for relevant keywords.

## Addressing Skill Gaps and Building Credibility

When highlighting transferable skills, acknowledge that you may not have every qualification listed in a job posting—and that's perfectly normal. Focus on demonstrating your ability to learn quickly and adapt to new challenges. If you lack specific technical skills, emphasize your problem-solving abilities and provide examples of how you've successfully learned new systems or processes in the past. Include any relevant certifications, online courses, or self-directed learning that shows initiative in developing new competencies. For significant career changes, consider creating a functional or combination resume format that emphasizes skills over chronological work history. However, be prepared to provide specific examples during interviews that substantiate your claims. Avoid overstating your abilities—instead, frame your skills honestly while showing enthusiasm for applying them in new contexts. For instance, 'Eager to apply proven project coordination and stakeholder management skills in a marketing environment' shows both confidence and appropriate humility. Consider including a brief professional summary that explicitly addresses your career transition and positions your transferable skills as assets that bring fresh perspective to the role. This proactive approach demonstrates self-awareness and strategic thinking—qualities that employers highly value.

## Key Takeaways

- Transferable skills are your professional superpowers—they work across industries and roles, making you adaptable and valuable to employers

- Map your skills strategically by analyzing job descriptions and using the employer's language to describe your relevant experiences

- Use the CAR method (Context, Action, Result) to transform generic skill statements into compelling, quantified achievements

- Draw examples from all life experiences—volunteer work, education, hobbies, and personal projects all demonstrate valuable skills

- Address career transitions proactively by emphasizing your ability to learn quickly and bring fresh perspective to new roles

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do I identify transferable skills if I've only had one type of job?

Look beyond your job title to the specific tasks you performed—managing schedules, training new employees, handling customer complaints, or improving processes all demonstrate transferable skills. Also consider volunteer work, education, hobbies, and personal projects that required planning, communication, or problem-solving abilities.

### Should I use a functional resume format to highlight transferable skills?

While functional formats can emphasize skills over work history, many employers and ATS systems prefer chronological or combination formats. Instead, weave transferable skills into your traditional work experience section and include a 'Core Competencies' section at the top of your resume.

### How many transferable skills should I include on my resume?

Focus on 8-12 core transferable skills that are most relevant to your target role. Quality trumps quantity—it's better to provide strong examples for fewer skills than to list many skills without substantiation. Tailor this list for each application based on the job requirements.

# How to List Volunteer Experience on Your Resume | aNewJob.com

Source: https://anewjob.com/resume-guide/volunteer-experience-resume

# How to List Volunteer Experience on Your Resume

Volunteer experience is often an untapped goldmine on resumes, yet many job seekers struggle with how to present it effectively. Whether you're a recent graduate looking to fill experience gaps, a career changer seeking to demonstrate transferable skills, or a seasoned professional wanting to showcase your community involvement, volunteer work can significantly strengthen your candidacy. Research shows that 82% of hiring managers view volunteer experience favorably, and 85% are more likely to hire candidates who volunteer. The key lies in strategically positioning your volunteer work to highlight relevant skills, demonstrate your values, and show your commitment to making a positive impact. When properly presented, volunteer experience can showcase leadership abilities, technical skills, project management capabilities, and cultural fit – all while differentiating you from other candidates. This guide will walk you through exactly how to transform your volunteer activities into compelling resume content that resonates with employers.

## In This Article

- Where to Place Volunteer Experience on Your Resume

- How to Format and Structure Volunteer Entries

- Highlighting Relevant Skills and Achievements

- Common Mistakes to Avoid When Listing Volunteer Work

- Key Takeaways

- FAQ

## Where to Place Volunteer Experience on Your Resume

The placement of your volunteer experience depends on its relevance to your target role and your overall work history. For recent graduates or career changers, create a dedicated 'Volunteer Experience' section immediately after your professional experience or education section. This positioning treats volunteer work with the same importance as paid positions. If your volunteer work is highly relevant to the job you're seeking, consider integrating it within your main 'Professional Experience' section. For example, if you're applying for a marketing role and managed social media for a nonprofit, list this alongside your paid marketing positions. Use clear labels like 'Volunteer Marketing Coordinator' to maintain transparency. For experienced professionals with extensive work history, volunteer experience can be placed in a separate section toward the bottom of your resume, or highlighted in a 'Community Involvement' section. However, if the volunteer role demonstrates leadership or skills directly applicable to your target position, consider featuring it more prominently. The key is ensuring the placement supports your overall narrative and doesn't overshadow critical professional experience while still showcasing the value you bring.

## How to Format and Structure Volunteer Entries

Format volunteer experience using the same structure as professional positions to maintain consistency and professionalism. Start with your volunteer title, followed by the organization name, location, and dates of service. Use action-oriented bullet points to describe your responsibilities and achievements, just as you would for paid positions. Example format: Volunteer Marketing Coordinator | Local Animal Shelter | City, State | Jan 2022 - Present • Developed social media strategy that increased follower engagement by 45% and adoptions by 20% • Coordinated fundraising events generating $15,000 in donations over six months • Managed team of 8 volunteers for monthly community outreach programs Quantify your impact whenever possible using specific metrics, percentages, or dollar amounts. Instead of writing 'helped with fundraising,' specify 'organized silent auction that raised $5,000 for youth programs.' Focus on transferable skills that align with your career goals – leadership, project management, communication, technical abilities, or industry-specific expertise. Treat volunteer roles with the same level of detail and professionalism as paid positions, demonstrating that you bring the same dedication and results-oriented approach to all your commitments.

## Highlighting Relevant Skills and Achievements

Transform volunteer activities into compelling evidence of your professional capabilities by focusing on skills that transfer to your target role. Analyze the job description to identify key requirements, then showcase how your volunteer work demonstrates these competencies. For instance, organizing charity events translates to project management, event coordination, and stakeholder communication skills. Emphasize leadership roles and progressive responsibility. If you started as a volunteer and became a team lead or board member, highlight this progression to show your ability to take initiative and earn trust. Technical skills gained through volunteer work – such as database management, graphic design, or website development – are particularly valuable and should be prominently featured. Focus on results and impact rather than just duties. Instead of 'participated in food drives,' write 'coordinated monthly food drives serving 200+ families and managed inventory tracking system.' Highlight any recognition, awards, or special projects that demonstrate exceptional performance. Include cross-functional collaboration, budget management, training others, or implementing new processes. These experiences often provide unique opportunities to develop skills that paid positions might not offer, such as working with diverse populations, managing limited resources creatively, or driving change in established organizations. Present these challenges as valuable learning experiences that enhanced your professional toolkit.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid When Listing Volunteer Work

One of the biggest mistakes is underselling volunteer experience by using vague descriptions or minimal detail. Avoid generic phrases like 'helped out' or 'assisted with various tasks.' Instead, be specific about your role, responsibilities, and impact. Don't assume employers will understand the significance of your contributions – spell out the value you created. Avoid listing every volunteer activity you've ever done. Be selective and include only experiences that strengthen your candidacy for the specific role. Including a one-time volunteer day from five years ago may dilute the impact of more substantial, relevant experiences. Quality over quantity is essential. Never exaggerate your role or responsibilities. If you were part of a team, don't claim sole credit for team achievements. Use collaborative language when appropriate: 'contributed to team effort that resulted in...' rather than claiming individual ownership of group successes. Don't forget to keep volunteer experience current and relevant. Remove outdated entries that no longer serve your professional narrative, and regularly update ongoing volunteer roles with new achievements. Finally, avoid controversial organizations or causes that might create bias, unless they're directly relevant to your target industry. Focus on universally respected causes or highlight the professional skills gained rather than the cause itself when in doubt.

## Key Takeaways

- Place volunteer experience strategically based on its relevance to your target role and career stage

- Format volunteer entries with the same professional structure as paid positions, including quantified achievements

- Focus on transferable skills and measurable impact rather than just listing duties or activities

- Be selective and include only volunteer experiences that strengthen your candidacy for specific roles

- Avoid underselling volunteer work – treat it as valuable professional experience that demonstrates your capabilities

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Should I include short-term or one-time volunteer activities on my resume?

Generally, focus on ongoing or substantial volunteer commitments rather than one-time events. However, include short-term activities if they're highly relevant to your target role or demonstrate significant skills and achievements.

### How far back should I go when listing volunteer experience?

Follow the same general rule as work experience – typically 10-15 years maximum. However, include older volunteer work if it's highly relevant to your current career goals or demonstrates long-term commitment to a cause related to your field.

### Can I list volunteer work in my professional experience section alongside paid jobs?

Yes, if the volunteer role is highly relevant to your target position and involved substantial responsibilities. Clearly label it as volunteer work and format it consistently with your paid positions to maintain transparency and professionalism.

# Warehouse & Logistics Resume | Resume Guide | aNewJob.com

Source: https://anewjob.com/resume-guide/warehouse-logistics-resume-forklift-inventory-safety

Industries

# Warehouse and Logistics Resume: Forklift, Inventory, Safety

Warehouse and logistics managers usually need people fast, and they skim. They look for the equipment you can run, the systems you know, how you handle safety, and whether you show up and keep pace. This guide shows how to put those things on one page so they are easy to find, with sample wording you can adapt.

## In This Article

- What a warehouse hiring manager looks for in the first few seconds

- How to list forklift and equipment skills

- Showing inventory and systems experience

- Putting safety on the page without sounding generic

- Pace, reliability, and leadership: the numbers that matter

- Layout, length, and mistakes to avoid

- Key Takeaways

- FAQ

## What a warehouse hiring manager looks for in the first few seconds

Most warehouse resumes get a quick look, often on a phone or between other tasks. The reader is checking a short list: Can this person operate the equipment we have? Have they done this kind of work (receiving, picking, packing, shipping, inventory)? Are they safe? Can they work our shift? If those answers are easy to find at the top of the page, you get a closer read. Put a short summary under your name, then a skills or equipment block, then your work history. A summary can be two or three lines: "Warehouse associate with 4 years in receiving and order picking. Certified sit-down and stand-up forklift operator. Experienced with RF scanners and warehouse management systems. Clean safety record. Available for first or second shift." That one paragraph answers the main screening questions. If you are applying to a specific posting, use its words. If it says "material handler" and you have been calling yourself a "warehouse worker," write "material handler" where it is true. The keywords guide covers how to match a posting without stuffing. If you have a long gap or a string of short temp jobs, don't hide it, but don't dwell on it either. A staffing agency job counts as real experience. List the agency as the employer and the client site underneath, or the other way around, and be consistent.

## How to list forklift and equipment skills

"Forklift" alone doesn't say much. There are different types, and employers hire for specific ones. Name what you have actually operated, for example: sit-down counterbalance forklift, stand-up reach truck, order picker (cherry picker), electric and manual pallet jack, walkie stacker, and clamp or turret trucks if you've used them. Add other gear too: pallet wrapper, box cutter and strapping tools, dock plates, conveyor systems, scissor lift. On certification, be accurate. Under OSHA rules, employers train and evaluate their own forklift operators, and operators are re-evaluated at least every three years. That means a "forklift license" from a previous employer may not transfer automatically, but it still shows you have the training and experience, and many employers will accept it or retrain you quickly. List it like this: - Forklift Operator Certification (sit-down and stand-up), issued by [employer or training provider], 2023 - OSHA-compliant powered industrial truck training, [year] If your certification has lapsed, you can still write "Forklift operator, 3 years of experience (recertification needed)" or leave the certification line off and put the experience in your bullets. Don't list a current certification you don't hold. Employers usually check, and it ends the conversation. Other credentials worth listing if you have them: hazmat or DOT training, first aid/CPR, and a CDL if you drive. The certifications article covers formatting in more detail.

## Showing inventory and systems experience

Inventory work is about accuracy, and hiring managers want proof you can be trusted with it. Say what you did and what system you used. Common terms to include when they're true: cycle counts, physical inventory, receiving against purchase orders, bills of lading (BOL), putaway, picking and packing, FIFO, cross-docking, replenishment, returns processing, labeling, and RF or barcode scanning. Name the systems. A "warehouse management system (WMS)" is the general term, but if you used something specific, such as SAP, Oracle, Manhattan, NetSuite, or a company's own system, write it. Include basic tools too: Excel for tracking, handheld scanners, label printers, and shipping software. Sample bullets: - Received and put away 40-60 pallets per shift using RF scanner and WMS, checking counts against purchase orders and reporting shortages the same day - Performed weekly cycle counts in a 12,000-sq-ft stockroom and corrected location errors in the system - Picked and packed orders from pick lists, checking item, quantity, and label before sending to shipping - Loaded and unloaded trailers, verified paperwork against freight, and noted damage on the BOL before sign-off Use numbers you know or can reasonably estimate: pallets per shift, orders per day, size of the building, number of SKUs, truck count. Use "about" or a range if you aren't sure. Don't make up an accuracy rate. If you were told your pick accuracy or counts were consistently on target, say that in plain words.

## Putting safety on the page without sounding generic

Almost every warehouse resume says "safety-conscious." It means nothing without an example. Safety shows up better as specific actions: what you inspected, what you reported, what rules you followed, and what you trained others on. Useful wording, if it's true for you: - Completed daily forklift pre-shift inspections and tagged equipment out of service when problems were found - Followed lockout/tagout, PPE, and hazard communication procedures - Kept aisles and dock areas clear and reported spills and damaged racking to the supervisor - Worked [number] years/months without a recordable incident or lost-time injury - Trained new hires on pallet jack use and safe stacking - Took part in weekly safety meetings and near-miss reporting Only claim a clean record if you know it's accurate. If you were involved in an incident and have since been retrained, you don't need to bring it up on the resume. Be ready to answer honestly if asked. Safety goes beyond the safety bullets, too. Careful loading, accurate labeling, and proper lifting all count. A bullet like "Stacked and wrapped mixed pallets to company standard, with no product damage reported in transit" shows safety and quality together.

## Pace, reliability, and leadership: the numbers that matter

Warehouses run on throughput and attendance. If you can show you worked at a steady pace, include it. Examples: units per hour, lines picked per shift, trailers unloaded per day, orders shipped per week, or how your numbers compared to a target ("consistently met daily pick rate"). Don't copy the numbers in these examples. Use your own, or leave the number out and describe the result. - Met or exceeded the daily pick-rate target in most weeks while keeping errors low - Unloaded 3-4 containers per shift as part of a two-person team - Cross-trained in receiving, shipping, and inventory control, and covered absences on all three - Worked peak season overtime and weekend shifts with perfect attendance for the season If you've led people, even informally, say so: "Lead on second-shift loading team of 6," "Trained 10+ new hires," "Assigned daily tasks and tracked completion." Supervisor and lead roles are often filled from within, so this matters even if you didn't have the title. For logistics roles beyond the floor, such as dispatcher, shipping coordinator, or inventory control clerk, add the paperwork and communication side: carrier scheduling, freight documentation, customer or vendor contact, and discrepancy resolution. Show you can keep records straight and talk to drivers and customers without drama.

## Layout, length, and mistakes to avoid

One page is enough for most warehouse jobs. Use a plain layout with clear headings: Summary, Skills and Equipment, Certifications, Work Experience, Education. Keep to standard fonts and avoid tables, text boxes, or graphics that confuse application systems. Save as a PDF unless the posting asks for Word. For each job, list employer, city and state, job title, and dates, then 3-5 bullets. Start bullets with verbs like loaded, received, picked, counted, operated, trained, and inspected. Common mistakes: listing every duty with no result, using "responsible for" in every line, leaving off the type of equipment, and burying certifications at the bottom. Also avoid skill ratings and "hard worker" claims. Show it with attendance, pace, and what you were trusted to do. Check that dates are right, since many warehouse employers verify them. If you already have old resumes, pay stubs, training certificates, or performance reviews, those hold most of what you need. aNewJob can build the resume from documents you already have by asking you a few questions to fill the gaps. Whichever way you write it, read it once as a hiring manager would: can you tell in ten seconds what you can operate, what you've handled, and when you can start?

## Key Takeaways

- Put equipment, certifications, and shift availability near the top so a quick skim answers the main screening questions.

- Name the exact equipment you've run (sit-down, stand-up, reach truck, order picker, pallet jack) instead of just writing "forklift."

- List forklift certification accurately, with who issued it and when. Never list one you don't currently hold.

- Name your systems and tasks: WMS, RF scanner, cycle counts, receiving against POs, BOLs, and putaway.

- Show safety through specific actions like inspections, reporting hazards, and training others, not through the word "safe."

- Use real numbers for pace and volume (pallets, orders, units per hour), and leave the number out if you don't know it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Should I put forklift certification on my resume if it expired?

Don't list it as current. You can write your years of forklift experience in your work history and summary, and note that you're ready to be recertified. Employers must train and evaluate operators themselves, so many will retrain you quickly if your experience is solid.

### How do I write a warehouse resume with no warehouse experience?

Use related work: retail stocking, receiving deliveries, food prep, moving or delivery jobs, or anything involving lifting, counting, and following schedules. Emphasize reliability, attendance, physical stamina, and any scanner or inventory tasks. Add any safety training you've taken, and keep the resume to one page.

### How do I list temp agency warehouse jobs?

List the staffing agency as the employer and the client site or company under it, or the reverse, as long as you do it the same way each time. Group several short assignments under one entry if the duties were similar, and show the total time span. This keeps the page clean and still shows steady work.

### What skills should I list for a warehouse job?

Include equipment you can operate, inventory and shipping tasks, systems you've used, and safety practices. Examples: forklift and pallet jack operation, order picking, cycle counting, RF scanning, WMS data entry, trailer loading, and lockout/tagout. Match the wording of the job posting where it's accurate.

# What is an ATS? How Applicant Tracking Systems Work | Resume Guide | aNewJob.com

Source: https://anewjob.com/resume-guide/what-is-ats-resume

ATS

# What is an ATS? How Applicant Tracking Systems Work

An Applicant Tracking System (ATS) is software that employers use to collect, scan, and rank job applications before human recruiters ever see them. Understanding how these systems work is crucial for modern job seekers, as over 75% of resumes are rejected by ATS software before reaching hiring managers.

## In This Article

- What is an Applicant Tracking System?

- How ATS Resume Screening Works

- Common ATS Challenges and Pitfalls

- How to Optimize Your Resume for ATS Success

- Key Takeaways

- FAQ

## What is an Applicant Tracking System?

An Applicant Tracking System is a software application that enables companies to electronically handle their recruitment and hiring processes. Think of an ATS as a digital gatekeeper that automatically sorts through hundreds or thousands of resumes to identify the most qualified candidates for a position. These systems serve multiple functions beyond resume screening. They help employers post job openings across multiple platforms, manage candidate communications, schedule interviews, and maintain databases of potential hires. Popular ATS platforms include Workday, Greenhouse, BambooHR, and Taleo, each with slightly different algorithms and capabilities. For job seekers, the most important function of an ATS is resume parsing and keyword matching. When you submit your resume through a company's online portal, the ATS immediately scans your document, extracts relevant information, and assigns it a compatibility score based on how well it matches the job requirements.

## How ATS Resume Screening Works

The ATS resume screening process begins the moment you hit 'submit' on a job application. First, the system parses your resume, converting it into a standardized format and extracting key information like your contact details, work experience, education, and skills. This parsing process can sometimes struggle with complex formatting, graphics, or unusual fonts. Next, the ATS performs keyword matching by comparing your resume content against the job description. It looks for specific terms, phrases, job titles, skills, and qualifications that the employer has deemed important. For example, if a job posting mentions 'project management,' 'Agile methodology,' and 'stakeholder communication,' the ATS will search your resume for these exact phrases or related variations. Finally, the system ranks candidates based on their compatibility scores. Those with the highest scores – typically the top 10-25% – are forwarded to human recruiters for review. The rest may be automatically rejected or placed in a holding database for future consideration. This ranking system explains why two similarly qualified candidates might receive vastly different responses to their applications.

## Common ATS Challenges and Pitfalls

Many qualified candidates unknowingly sabotage their chances by submitting resumes that ATS software cannot properly read or interpret. Complex formatting is the biggest culprit – resumes with multiple columns, text boxes, headers and footers, or embedded images often confuse parsing algorithms, causing important information to be missed or misinterpreted. File format issues also create problems. While PDFs preserve formatting better for human readers, some older ATS platforms struggle with PDF parsing. Conversely, Word documents (.doc or .docx) are generally more ATS-friendly but may display differently across devices. Creative resume designs with graphics, charts, or unusual layouts might look impressive to humans but are virtually invisible to most ATS software. Keyword stuffing represents another common mistake. Some job seekers try to game the system by cramming irrelevant keywords into their resumes, often in white text or hidden sections. Modern ATS platforms are sophisticated enough to detect these tactics, and they can actually hurt your ranking. Instead, focus on naturally incorporating relevant keywords from the job description throughout your experience descriptions and skills sections.

## How to Optimize Your Resume for ATS Success

Creating an ATS-friendly resume starts with using a clean, simple format with standard fonts like Arial, Calibri, or Times New Roman. Stick to a single-column layout with clear section headings like 'Professional Experience,' 'Education,' and 'Skills.' Use standard bullet points and avoid tables, text boxes, or graphics that might confuse the parsing software. Keyword optimization requires careful analysis of job descriptions. Identify the most important skills, qualifications, and requirements mentioned in the posting, then naturally incorporate these terms throughout your resume. For instance, if a job requires 'customer relationship management,' use that exact phrase rather than abbreviating it as 'CRM' – though including both variations can be beneficial. Tailor your resume for each application by adjusting your professional summary, skills section, and experience descriptions to match the specific role. Use the same language and terminology found in the job posting. If the employer mentions 'budget management,' use that phrase instead of 'financial oversight.' This targeted approach significantly improves your ATS compatibility score and demonstrates genuine interest in the specific position.

## Key Takeaways

- Use simple, single-column formatting with standard fonts to ensure proper ATS parsing

- Incorporate relevant keywords from job descriptions naturally throughout your resume content

- Save your resume in both .docx and PDF formats, but submit .docx when possible for better ATS compatibility

- Customize your resume for each application to match specific job requirements and terminology

- Avoid graphics, tables, and complex formatting that can confuse ATS software and cause parsing errors

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What percentage of companies use ATS software?

Approximately 99% of Fortune 500 companies and 70% of all employers use some form of ATS software to manage their hiring processes. This makes ATS optimization essential for modern job seekers across all industries and company sizes.

### Should I submit my resume as a PDF or Word document?

Word documents (.docx) are generally more ATS-friendly and recommended when possible. However, if the job posting specifically requests PDFs or doesn't specify, a well-formatted PDF from a recent version of software usually works fine with modern ATS platforms.

### How can I tell if a company uses an ATS?

If you're applying through an online portal that asks you to upload your resume and then fill out additional forms with your information, the company likely uses an ATS. Most major job boards and corporate career pages are integrated with ATS software.

# The 10-Second Resume Scan | Resume Guide | aNewJob.com

Source: https://anewjob.com/resume-guide/what-recruiters-look-at-first-10-seconds

Basics

# What Recruiters Look at in the First 10 Seconds of a Resume

When a recruiter has a stack of resumes to get through, the first look is a quick skim, not a careful read. "Ten seconds" is a rule of thumb, not a stopwatch measurement, but the point holds: a few spots on your page decide whether someone keeps reading. This guide covers those spots and how to set each one up.

## In This Article

- What the first look is really for

- The top of the page: name, contact info and a short opening

- Job titles, employers and dates

- The first bullets under your most recent job

- Layout that makes the scan easy

- A quick way to test your own resume

- Key Takeaways

- FAQ

## What the first look is really for

In the first skim, the recruiter is not judging your whole career. They are asking one question: does this person look like a match for the job I'm filling? They want a fast yes, a fast no, or a "maybe, read more." Your goal is to make the yes easy to see. That means the match has to show up without effort. If a recruiter has to read three paragraphs to work out that you've been a dispatcher for six years, you may not get the third paragraph. The information they need first is your most recent job title, where you worked, roughly how long, and a couple of proof points that line up with the posting. Before you change anything, pull up the job posting and pick out the three or four things it clearly asks for. Everything below is about making those things visible in the first few seconds.

## The top of the page: name, contact info and a short opening

The eye starts at the top. Your name should be the largest text on the page, followed by a city and state, a phone number, a professional-sounding email address, and a LinkedIn link if you have one. Skip the full street address. An email like jsmith.dispatch@gmail.com reads better than one with a nickname or birth year. Directly under the header, a two- or three-line summary can tell the recruiter who you are before they scan anything else. It works when it names your role, your experience level and one or two things the job cares about. For example: Operations coordinator with 6 years in logistics and dispatch. Schedule 40+ drivers daily, manage carrier relationships, and cut late deliveries by using route and load data. Experienced with Samsara and Excel. It doesn't work when it's vague: "Hard-working professional seeking a challenging opportunity." That could describe anyone, so it tells the recruiter nothing. If you can't write a specific summary, leave it out and let the experience section do the work.

## Job titles, employers and dates

After the top of the page, most people's eyes drop down the left side, picking up job titles, company names and dates. This is where a recruiter builds a quick picture of your path: what you've done, where, and for how long. Make that picture clean. List jobs in reverse chronological order, put the job title first and in bold, and format dates the same way every time (for example, "Mar 2021 – Present"). If your official title is an internal code, such as "Associate III," write what the job actually was and keep the official title beside it: "Customer Support Specialist (Associate III)." Don't change your level or invent a title you never held, since employers can check. If you have a gap, don't try to hide it with odd formatting. A recruiter who sees clear years and a short note, like "Career break for family caregiving, 2022–2023," usually moves on. A confusing timeline makes them stop and wonder.

## The first bullets under your most recent job

If the title and dates look right, the next stop is usually the first two or three bullets under your current or most recent job. Those lines get read far more than anything buried on page two, so put your strongest, most relevant points first, not the duties you did every day. Compare these two versions of the same job: Before: Responsible for answering customer calls and emails and resolving issues. After: Resolved 50+ customer calls and emails per day, keeping satisfaction scores above 90% for 18 months in a row. The second one shows scale, a result and a time frame. If you don't have exact numbers, use honest estimates you could defend in an interview, such as "about 30 orders a shift" or "a team of 5." Don't make up figures. If the job posting stresses a specific skill, such as scheduling, cash handling or Spanish fluency, make sure one of those top bullets shows it.

## Layout that makes the scan easy

Even great content gets skipped if the page is hard to scan. Use a plain, readable font at a normal size, clear section headings (Summary, Experience, Skills, Education), and enough white space that the page doesn't look like a wall of text. Keep bullets to one or two lines each, with no more than five or six under a job, and fewer for older roles. Avoid things that slow the eye down or break when a file is opened on a different computer: photos, multiple columns packed with text, skill-rating bars, tiny fonts, and long paragraphs. A skills section is fine and useful, but keep it as a short, simple list of real skills the job asks for. Length matters less than clarity. One page is plenty for many people, and two pages is fine if the second page is earning its place. What counts is that the most important material sits in the top half of page one.

## A quick way to test your own resume

Set a timer for ten seconds, look at your resume, then look away and write down what you remember. Better yet, hand it to a friend, then ask what job you do, where you've worked recently and what you seem good at. If they can't answer, that tells you what to fix. Also run through this short checklist. Is your name clear and your contact info complete? Does your most recent job title match, or at least relate to, the job you're applying for? Are the dates easy to follow? Do the first bullets show results instead of duties? Does anything on the page look crowded or confusing? If you have old resumes, performance reviews or job descriptions lying around but don't want to start from scratch, aNewJob can build your resume from those documents through a short interview. Either way, make the check above part of every application, since each posting asks for slightly different things.

## Key Takeaways

- The first skim is a quick match check: does this person look right for this job?

- Put a clear name, city and state, phone, and professional email at the top, with a specific two- or three-line summary if you use one.

- Make job titles, employers and dates easy to follow, in reverse chronological order with consistent formatting.

- Lead each recent job with your strongest, most relevant bullets, using real numbers or defensible estimates.

- Use a plain layout with clear headings and white space, and skip photos, rating bars and dense paragraphs.

- Test your resume by showing it to a friend for ten seconds and asking what they remember.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Do recruiters really spend only 10 seconds on a resume?

It's a rule of thumb, not an exact number. Time varies by recruiter, role and how many applicants there are, but the first look is usually a fast skim. Plan for a quick scan first and a careful read only if you pass it.

### What is the most important part of a resume?

There isn't a single part, but the top half of page one carries the most weight. That's where your name, recent job title, dates and first bullets sit, and together they show whether you fit the role.

### Should I put a summary at the top of my resume?

A short, specific summary helps if it names your role, experience and a few things the job asks for. If it would only contain general phrases like "hard-working team player," skip it and let your experience speak.

### Does the 10-second scan also apply to online applications?

Yes. Even when an applicant tracking system sorts resumes first, a person usually looks at the ones that make the cut, and that look is quick. Write for both by using a clean layout and the words from the job posting.

# What to Include on a Resume: Essential Sections | Resume Guide | aNewJob.com

Basics

# What to Include on a Resume: Essential Sections

Creating an effective resume starts with understanding which resume sections to include and what content belongs in each one. Knowing what to put on resume can make the difference between landing an interview and getting overlooked by hiring managers and applicant tracking systems.

## In This Article

- Essential Header Information and Contact Details

- Professional Summary or Profile Statement

- Work Experience and Professional Accomplishments

- Education, Skills, and Additional Relevant Sections

- Key Takeaways

- FAQ

## Essential Header Information and Contact Details

Your resume header serves as your professional introduction and must include specific contact information that makes it easy for employers to reach you. Start with your full name in a larger, bold font, followed by your phone number, professional email address, and city/state (full address is no longer necessary for privacy reasons). Include your LinkedIn profile URL and relevant professional website or portfolio link if applicable. Avoid outdated elements like objective statements in your header area, and never include personal information such as age, marital status, photo, or social security number. Your email address should be professional—ideally some variation of your name rather than nicknames or numbers. If your current email seems unprofessional, create a new one specifically for job searching. This header section, while brief, creates the first impression and ensures hiring managers can contact you easily.

## Professional Summary or Profile Statement

A well-crafted professional summary replaces the outdated objective statement and provides a compelling snapshot of your qualifications in 2-4 sentences. This resume section should highlight your years of experience, key skills, and most relevant achievements that align with your target position. For example: 'Results-driven marketing professional with 5+ years of experience developing digital campaigns that increased brand awareness by 40% and generated $2M in revenue.' Tailor this section to each job application by incorporating keywords from the job description and emphasizing the qualifications most relevant to the specific role. Entry-level candidates can focus on education, internships, relevant coursework, and transferable skills from part-time work or volunteer experience. Mid-career professionals should emphasize quantifiable achievements and specialized expertise, while senior-level candidates should highlight leadership experience and strategic accomplishments.

## Work Experience and Professional Accomplishments

The work experience section typically carries the most weight in hiring decisions and should showcase your professional growth and achievements. List positions in reverse chronological order, including job title, company name, location, and employment dates. For each role, include 3-5 bullet points that focus on accomplishments rather than just job duties, using action verbs and quantifiable results whenever possible. Structure each bullet point using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) when possible. For example: 'Managed a team of 8 sales representatives and implemented new training protocols, resulting in a 25% increase in quarterly sales revenue.' Include relevant experience from the past 10-15 years, though recent graduates may include internships, part-time work, and significant volunteer roles. Avoid lengthy paragraphs and focus on achievements that demonstrate skills relevant to your target position.

## Education, Skills, and Additional Relevant Sections

Your education section should include degree type, major, institution name, graduation year, and GPA if it's 3.5 or higher and you're a recent graduate. List education after work experience unless you're a recent graduate or changing careers where your degree is particularly relevant. Include relevant coursework, academic honors, or projects only if they directly support your candidacy for the target role. Create a dedicated skills section that includes both hard and soft skills relevant to your industry, using keywords from job descriptions. Organize skills into categories like 'Technical Skills,' 'Software Proficiency,' or 'Languages' for better readability. Additional sections might include certifications, professional associations, volunteer work, publications, or relevant projects—but only include these if they strengthen your candidacy. Keep the focus on what's most relevant to your target position, and remember that every section should add value to your overall professional narrative.

## Key Takeaways

- Include essential contact information in your header but avoid personal details like age or marital status

- Write a compelling professional summary that highlights your most relevant qualifications and achievements

- Focus on accomplishments rather than job duties in your work experience section, using quantifiable results

- Tailor your resume content to match keywords and requirements from the specific job description

- Only include additional sections like volunteer work or hobbies if they directly support your candidacy

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How long should my resume be?

Most resumes should be one page for entry-level positions and up to two pages for experienced professionals. Focus on relevance rather than length—include only information that strengthens your candidacy for the specific role.

### Should I include references on my resume?

No, don't include references or 'references available upon request' on your resume. This information takes up valuable space and references are typically requested later in the hiring process if needed.

### What if I have employment gaps in my work history?

Address employment gaps honestly by using years only instead of months for dates, and consider including relevant activities during gaps such as education, volunteer work, or freelance projects that maintained your skills.
